video_title: The Russian Military Beyond 2026 - Pain Points, Potential & Lessons for NATO (with Michael Kofman)
gist: Second part of Perun's interview with Michael Kofman projecting the Russian military to 2027 and beyond: infantry and air fleet strain, stabilized armor, rapidly scaling drone and missile strike, post-war shrinkage constrained by budget, industry and demographics, and what NATO should adapt to.

themes.theme: Russian ground forces: infantry strain, stabilized armor

insights.claim: Russian assault infantry capability is likely trending down: Ukrainian claimed Russian casualties hit multi-year highs in October 2026 (about 2,100 in a day on 19 October, then reportedly broken again), and recruitment claims do not reconcile with the authorized force growth and budget payments.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Infantry quality, not equipment, is the binding Russian ground-force constraint into 2027.

insights.claim: Russian heavy equipment has stabilized: visually confirmed losses in 2026 are well below 2022-2024, destroyed vehicles skew more modern (T-90M rather than T-55/T-62), and refurbished armor is reappearing in storage yards and going to the National Guard.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Russia consciously cut frontline heavy-equipment exposure to a sustainable loss rate, so Ukraine should not expect armor shortages in 2027.

insights.claim: Russia has lost the giant Soviet-era equipment reserve that let it absorb early losses and expand the force, but with current employment, heavy equipment quality is likely to stay static or slightly improve through 2027.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The strategic hedge is spent for any future war even if the current war is sustainable.

insights.claim: Fire and strike, not tank upgrades, is what should worry NATO: the T-80BV to T-80BVM to T-90M modernization treadmill is not what kept Western defense circles up at night.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Focusing on Russian armor quality misdirects NATO threat assessment from drones, missiles and strike.
insights.quote: people focus on this too much

themes.theme: VKS air power: tricks learned, fleet wearing down

insights.claim: Russian airframe numbers are under strain: Justin Bronk's RUSI comparison of confirmed losses vs deliveries (late 2020 to late 2025) shows Su-34 about +10, Su-57 and Su-35 growing, but bombers and Su-30 shrinking, and Su-25, MiG-31 and Tu-160 lines cannot offset losses and flight-hour wear.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Russia must spend heavily on aviation just to stand still, a mixed picture for 2027-28.

insights.claim: A Russian source (Fighter Bomber) says Ukraine's small air force plus drones keeps Russian fighters on duty around the clock at thousands of flight hours per year per aircraft, driving failures and repairs; aviation has no fast regeneration path unlike ground forces.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Wear-out, not only combat losses, erodes Russian air fleet size.

insights.claim: Russia's strategic air campaign misread the 1991/1999/2003 US-led precedents: precision strike worked there only because of air superiority and large-scale air employment, so Russia built a 'cheap knockoff' without the underlying air-power concept or training.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Explains why early Russian strikes failed to paralyze Ukraine's economy or will.
insights.quote: cheap version knockoff of a Rolex watch

insights.claim: Russian air power still operates mostly in singles and pairs, glide-bomb use is battlefield preparation rather than responsive close air support, and there has been no real improvement in SEAD/DEAD; Ukrainian air defenses are handled by saturation and exhaustion.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Ukraine should not expect a sudden Russian air capability jump in 2027; no warning-free leap in SEAD is plausible.

insights.claim: Russia's weak SEAD investment can be seen as a rational prioritization (NATO lacks ground-based air defense in its force structure and relies on superior air power), but in hindsight retaining many attack aircraft justified more investment in making the environment permissive.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Doctrine built for an NATO-opponent scenario left the VKS unprepared against Ukraine's large ground-based air defense park.

insights.claim: Russian one-way attack drone contracting ramped from about 2,500 in 2023 to 21,000 in 2024, 78,000 in 2025 and a 2026 target of 127,000; Kofman cites a procurement order of around 120,000 plus including decoys.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Strike mass is growing roughly an order of magnitude every year or two, outpacing interceptor supply.

insights.claim: Ukraine faces roughly 7,500 long-range drones monthly, close to 30% decoys, with over half of strikes now jet-powered Gerans; interception of propeller types was high 80s to near 90% while jet-powered ones face an intercept rate near 60%.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Interception rates are falling as Russia upgrades the threat mix, raising interceptor demand into winter and 2027.

insights.claim: Russian missile output is rising more shallowly: Ukrainian sources put combined cruise and ballistic missile production at about 2,100 in 2022, 2,500 in 2025 and 2,900 planned in 2026, with 1,300 ballistic and 1,600 cruise missiles targeted this year.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Missile quantity is a smaller lever than drones, but combined salvos are becoming more complex.

insights.claim: Russia is using Geran seekers for dynamic targeting hundreds of kilometers in depth against moving targets and combining ballistic, cruise, one-way drones and a growing arsenal of light cruise missiles, likely a major challenge next year.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Mini cruise missiles plus remote-operated drones raise the quality of the strike threat, not just quantity.

insights.claim: Russia is expanding capabilities beyond the front: the Buran-Aist satellite constellation could give some connectivity over Ukraine in 2027-28, and nuclear submarine production continues despite a weakened Black Sea surface fleet.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Space and sub-surface programs are modest positives for Russia, mostly not Ukraine-relevant.

themes.theme: Post-war Russian military: leadership, industry, budget, personnel

insights.claim: Gerasimov's 2022 force-expansion ideas predated the war and were not derived from combat experience; he reverted operational C2 to the pre-2010 setup and dismantled joint strategic commands, and his successors, drawn from officers who fought in Ukraine, may reverse these decisions.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Post-Gerasimov force design is an open variable; Russian reform historically goes 'two steps forward, one step back'.

insights.claim: For strategic planning, the safest assumption is that Russian leadership and learning improve, since analysts tend to assume worst-case adversary performance and internal Russian writing is more honest about shortcomings than outsiders believe.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Planning on Russian incompetence is a risky default; overconfidence is a 'slow and insidious killer'.

insights.claim: Russia's defense industrial boom is plateauing: Industry minister Alekanov said defense as 'locomotive of industrial growth' will soon reach maximum output, so continuing current models is cheaper than pivoting a highly indebted industry.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Economic incentives favor doubling down on existing designs (T-90M, 152mm artillery, Tu-160) over next-gen programs like Armata.

insights.claim: Budget limits will cap post-war Russian defense spending: staying above about 7% of GDP is unlikely to be realistic in the medium term without severe trade-offs, with deficits, business debt and deferred civilian spending accumulating; how the war ends (frozen lines with sanctions vs final deal with sanctions lifted) changes the funding picture massively.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Sanctions relief is the key swing factor for a rapid post-war Russian rearmament.

insights.claim: Russia's enlarged military will have to shrink after the war: it has been effectively stop-loss since September 2022, so many will leave once contracts are honored; official size is about 1.5 million, practical estimate 1.3-1.4 million.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Active-duty cuts are almost inevitable unless Russia restores two-year conscription (about +200,000 troops) or sustains costly bonuses.

insights.claim: Mediazona data on about 96,000 confirmed contract-soldier KIA show an average age of 42.3, most common bracket 48-50, and more killed aged 60+ than aged 18-20.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The demographic quality of the Russian infantry is poor and unattractive to retain after the war.

insights.claim: After the war, reserve infantry battalions and convict-manned assault companies are likely to go away, while drone specialists, the unmanned systems force and the advanced fire and strike component are likely to be retained.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Russian cuts will hit mass infantry first, preserving the capabilities most dangerous to NATO.
insights.quote: I can't imagine the specialists and the expertise

insights.claim: Russia's Unmanned Systems Forces targeted 168,000 personnel this year, a figure Kofman calls whimsical and unlikely to be reached, but it remains a very large component.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Drone force expansion is real but below announced goals.

themes.theme: Mass precision and what transfers to NATO and others

insights.claim: Mass precision can substitute for force density on defense (as low as about 15 men per kilometer) and deny terrain, but cannot create control; offensives still need boots on the ground, producing a commingled gray zone where presence does not confer control.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Drone-dense defenders can hold with few troops, which a manpower-short post-war Russia could copy.

insights.claim: Mass precision is a matter of force employment and organization (drone battalions, regiments, unmanned forces), not just owning drones, which is why Hezbollah is unlikely to achieve it despite using fiber-optic FPVs.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Possession of the technology without the structure and tactics will not replicate Russian-Ukrainian effects.

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone-equipped red forces repeatedly inflict heavy simulated losses on better-resourced NATO units in exercises, suggesting NATO has a real problem facing a pre-2022 style organization.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Exercise evidence supports NATO adaptation across breaching, logistics, C2 and infrastructure.

insights.claim: Post-war, Russia could stockpile one-way attack drones and cheap ground-launched cruise missiles and launch continuous waves from catapults or pickup trucks; a Geran-5 launch site reportedly took about 6 weeks to build, and defending with fixed-wing aircraft is the most expensive and least sustainable response.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Defender economics and NATO munition stocks (air-to-air and air-to-ground) do not match mass cheap salvos; Iranian drones already stressed French air-to-air missile inventories.

insights.claim: Air defense must be a layered ecosystem and high-low mix, not fixed-wing adaptation alone: drones fly at 30 m and 6-8,000 m, mass drones can also suppress tactical aviation, and airbase point defense is now a growing concern even for the US after events in CENTCOM's area earlier this year.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: NATO spending should include cheap interceptors, sensors and data fusion rather than only expensive platforms.

insights.claim: First movers in a military technology are not necessarily the best employers of it (tank and aircraft carrier precedents), and FPVs may not be decisive in a Pacific fight; outside observers like NATO or China, not under attack, can design better concepts, such as propeller carrier drones launching interceptor drones.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Observers have time and larger budgets to leapfrog Russia and Ukraine's improvised adaptations.

insights.claim: The structural outlook is that Russia struggles to keep pace in the longer-term industrial competition as European NATO spending rises, a significant Ukrainian military persists and Russian demographics age, but Russia will keep its recon-strike gains.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Europe's rearmament trajectory plus Ukraine's capacity should erode Russia's relative position after the 2020s, though the strike gap remains a near-term risk.
